## Workspace

The workspace itself: files that cannot be parsed or classified.

### LIT001

`parse-error`: A Python file in the workspace cannot be parsed.

No other rule can check a file that does not parse, so this finding hides
nothing: fix the syntax error and run the check again.

### LIT002

`unclassified-file`: A Python file matches no layer.

Every file in a package must belong to exactly one layer, because the other
rules are defined per layer. Move the file to a path the package layout
recognizes, extend the layout in `[layouts.<name>]`, or add an `[[overrides]]`
entry with a reason and an issue.

### LIT003

`manifest`: `leesh.toml` is invalid or out of date with the workspace.

Reported at `leesh.toml:1` for schema errors, unknown keys, overrides that
no longer match any file, overlapping overrides, and exceeded override
budgets. A manifest that cannot be loaded at all exits with status 2.

## Dependencies

What each layer and package may import.

### LIT101

`layer-dependency`: A module imports a layer its own layer may not depend on.

The allowed targets per layer come from `[layer_dependencies]`; by default
core imports only core, port imports core and port, shell adds shell,
adapter adds adapter, and routers import shell, boundary, router and
transaction modules.
Other layers are unrestricted, except that only test code may import test
code, so a composition root cannot wire a fake into production. A custom
layer uses its base layer's entry unless it has its own, and counts as its
base layer when imported. Imports are followed through package `__init__`
modules and re-exports, so a package initializer cannot launder a forbidden
dependency. Each forbidden module is reported once per importer. Declare
modules a layer may always use with `[[allowed_dependencies]]`, or record
one deliberate edge with `[[dependency_overrides]]`.

### LIT102

`forbidden-import`: A module imports a third-party package its layer may not use.

By default core and port modules may not import I/O clients (`httpx`,
`requests`, `redis`, `sqlite3`, `subprocess`, ...) or frameworks (`fastapi`,
`starlette`, `sqlalchemy`, `pydantic`, `pydantic_settings`); shell modules
may not import frameworks; routers may not import `sqlalchemy`. Set
`[forbidden_imports]` to replace a layer's list, or
`[extend_forbidden_imports]` to add to it. Every import statement counts,
including deferred and `TYPE_CHECKING` ones, and a workspace module that
re-exports a forbidden name is treated as that package.

### LIT103

`client-imports-server`: A client package imports a server package from the same workspace.

Packages with `kind = "client"` (SDKs, wire contracts) ship to consumers that
do not have the server installed. They may import libraries and other
clients, never modules owned by a `kind = "server"` package.

### LIT104

`cross-domain-import`: A domain imports another domain it does not declare, or that domain's internals.

A module under `<package>/domains/<name>/` belongs to domain `<name>`. It may
import another domain only when `[domains]` lists that domain among its
dependencies, and then only its core and shell modules (`core.py`,
`model.py`, `service.py`, ...); ports, adapters such as `persistence/`, and
boundaries stay private to their domain. Undeclared imports always fail,
so a workspace without `[domains]` keeps its domains independent. The
graph is checked when the manifest loads: every domain a dependency names
needs its own entry, and a cycle is a manifest error. `shared/`,
`projections/` and everything outside `domains/` are not domains. Imports
are followed through package `__init__` modules and re-exports, as for
LIT101, and `[[dependency_overrides]]` exempts one deliberate edge.

### LIT105

`import-cycle`: A workspace module participates in a circular import chain.

Modules form a directed acyclic graph. Circular imports couple modules
together and push code toward `TYPE_CHECKING` and local-import hacks.
Extract shared values into a lower module so imports flow one way.
`[[dependency_overrides]]` exempts one deliberate edge.

### LIT106

`deferred-import`: Code hides an import inside a function or a `TYPE_CHECKING` block.

Outside boundary and test modules, imports belong at module top level;
function-body imports obscure dependencies and paper over import cycles.
In core and port modules, `if TYPE_CHECKING:` blocks are also reported:
restructure shared types instead of hiding circular or cross-layer edges.

## Core purity

Core and port code computes from values it is given.

### LIT201

`nondeterminism`: Code reads the clock, randomness, or fresh IDs directly.

Core and port modules may not read any nondeterministic source
(`datetime.now`, `uuid4`, `random`, `secrets`, `os.urandom`) or use the
`time` module at all, `time.sleep` and `time.localtime` included; pass the
observed value in. Elsewhere only wall-clock reads are reported, so time
flows through one clock you can control in tests. List that clock's modules
in `workspace.clock_modules`; test modules are exempt. A custom layer with
`deterministic = true`, such as Temporal workflow code, is held to the core
standard.

### LIT202

`io-in-core`: Core or port code performs I/O.

Covers files and paths (`open`, `Path.read_text`, `shutil`, `tempfile`),
processes and the OS (`os.system`, `sys.exit`), standard streams, logging,
`print`/`input`, and any call into an I/O client package. Do the I/O in the
shell and pass the result into the core.

### LIT203

`ambient-state`: Code reads or writes state it was not given.

In core and port modules, reports process-wide context (working directory,
locale, decimal context, context variables) and `nonlocal` writes. Across
core, port, shell, adapter and router modules, reports `global` writes and
reads of mutable module-level collections, iterators, locks, queues, and
client singletons (`[]`, `defaultdict()`, `deque()`, `threading.Lock()`,
`httpx.Client()`, ...). Outside core (port, shell, adapter, router), also
reports stateful cache decorators (`@functools.cache`,
`@functools.lru_cache`); pure core functions may still memoize. Pass values
in and return the new state instead. Environment variables are covered by
LIT301.

### LIT204

`borrowed-mutation`: Core or port code mutates a value it received as an argument.

Tracks parameters, and aliases of them, through assignment, item and
attribute stores, `del`, augmented assignment, and mutating methods of
lists, dicts, sets and deques. Elements stay borrowed through loops,
`enumerate`, `zip`, `sorted`, `.values()`, `.items()`, `.get()`, and shallow
copies (`copy.copy`, `dataclasses.replace`, `.copy()`). On a value of unknown
type, a mutator such as `append` or `update` counts when its result is
discarded. Build and return a new value instead; the caller owns what it
passed in.

### LIT205

`frozen-values`: A core or port record is mutable.

Dataclasses must be declared with `frozen=True`. Their fields, and those
of a `NamedTuple`, may not be annotated with mutable collections (`list`,
`dict`, `set`, `bytearray`, `deque`, `defaultdict`, `OrderedDict`,
`Counter`, `ChainMap`, or the `typing` and `collections.abc` mutable
protocols), in string annotations too, or built by a `default_factory`
that returns one. `object.__setattr__` and `object.__delattr__` write to
frozen records and are reported everywhere except
`object.__setattr__(self, ...)` inside `__post_init__`, where it sets
derived fields. `ClassVar` fields are exempt. Use tuples, frozensets, or
read-only `Mapping`/`Sequence` interfaces.

### LIT206

`async-in-core`: Core code awaits or schedules concurrent work.

`await`, `async for`, `async with`, `asyncio` scheduling, threads and process
pools belong in the shell. The core computes a decision from values; the
shell decides when and how concurrently to carry it out.

### LIT207

`effectful-capability`: A core function takes a parameter that can perform effects.

Database sessions and connections, HTTP clients, file objects and
filesystems are capabilities: a function that receives one can do I/O even
when it imports nothing. Types are matched by exact resolved name, through
aliases, unions, `Optional`, `Annotated` and string annotations. Add your own
with `workspace.effectful_types`. Ports are exempt because they describe
effectful collaborators.

### LIT208

`dynamic-code`: Core or port code runs code or loads modules chosen at run time.

`eval`, `exec`, `compile`, `__import__`, `importlib.import_module`,
`globals`, `locals`, `breakpoint`, `setattr`, `delattr`, `vars`, `__dict__`,
dynamic `getattr` (with a non-literal attribute name), and `pickle`,
`marshal`, `shelve` and `runpy` execute or reach code no other rule can see,
so one call undoes every purity rule. Import the module and call the
function by name; parse serialized data at a boundary. `getattr` with a
literal name is read as the attribute it spells, so `getattr(os, "environ")`
is reported like `os.environ`.

### LIT209

`untyped-core`: Core or port code omits type annotations or uses untyped escape hatches.

Every parameter (except `self` and `cls`) and return type in core and port
modules must be annotated, because unannotated signatures hide capabilities
(LIT207) and boolean flags (LIT401). `Any`, unparameterized containers
(`dict`, `list`, `set`, `tuple`, `frozenset`, `Mapping`, `Sequence`), and
`TypedDict` classes are also reported: parse external data into typed
frozen dataclasses at a boundary.

## Edges

Effects that belong to one specific layer.

### LIT301

`environment-access`: Code outside the edges reads environment variables.

`os.environ`, `os.getenv` and their bytes variants, through any alias, are
allowed only in boundary, transaction and test modules. Read configuration
once at startup and pass typed values inward.

### LIT302

`transaction-boundary`: Code outside a transaction boundary calls `commit()` or `rollback()`.

One place per request or job decides when work is durable. Any method named
`commit` or `rollback` counts, unless its receiver resolves only to a
third-party package outside the database drivers and ORMs (`sqlalchemy`,
`asyncpg`, `psycopg`, `sqlite3`, ...), such as a search index writer. Only
transaction and test modules may call them.

### LIT303

`router-construction`: A router or shell constructs its own infrastructure.

Routers and shells receive repositories, clients, engines, adapters and
settings through dependency injection; they never build them. Calls to
anything named `*Repository`, `*Client` or `*Engine`, `create_engine`,
`create_async_engine`, `load_settings`, I/O client packages (`httpx`,
`requests`, `redis`, ...), or workspace adapter callables are reported,
matched by resolved name when the import is known.

### LIT304

`mocking`: A test patches code instead of passing fakes in.

Reports `unittest.mock`, pytest-mock fixtures (`mocker` and friends),
`monkeypatch` / `pytest.MonkeyPatch`, patching libraries (`freezegun`,
`time_machine`, `respx`, `responses`, `httpretty`, `mock`), and direct
module-attribute patching (`mod.attr = fake`, `setattr(mod, ...)`) in test
modules. If a test needs to replace a collaborator, the code under test
should accept it as a port; pass a hand-written fake that implements it.

### LIT305

`immutable-defaults`: A parameter default is not an immutable value.

Outside the edge layers (boundary, router, transaction, test), defaults may
only be literals, signed numbers, tuples, `UPPER_CASE` constants and enum
members, and immutable constructors such as `frozenset()` or `Decimal("0")`
over those. A same-module constant bound to a mutable value still counts as
mutable. A default such as
`[]`, `Settings()` or `datetime.now()` is evaluated once at import time and
hides a dependency; make the caller pass it. Protocol methods and exception
`__init__` methods are exempt.

### LIT306

`forbidden-call`: A module calls a function its layer may not call.

Nothing is forbidden by default. List qualified names per layer in
`[forbidden_calls]`, with a trailing `.*` for a whole module: for example
`time.sleep` and `asyncio.sleep` in Temporal workflow code, which must use
the workflow's own timer. Calls are matched by resolved name, so aliases
and `from` imports count. A custom layer inherits its base layer's list
unless it has its own.

### LIT307

`broad-except`: Code outside the edges swallows broad exceptions.

Bare `except:`, `except BaseException:`, and `except Exception:` hide bugs
and turn failures into silent wrong behavior. Outside boundary, router and
test modules, catch specific exception types or handle broad failures at
the edge. Handlers whose final statement is a `raise` (cleanup and re-raise
or error translation) are allowed.

### LIT308

`defensive-duck-typing`: Core or shell code uses duck-typing or type-cast workarounds.

`hasattr` and three-argument `getattr(obj, name, default)` in core and
shell, plus `typing.cast` in core, mask mismatched shapes instead of fixing
the data model. Parse values into typed dataclasses at the boundary and
narrow them explicitly.

### LIT309

`test-hygiene`: Tests sleep on real time, or (in strict mode) unit tests import adapters.

`time.sleep` makes tests slow and flaky; inject a clock or synchronize
explicitly. With `workspace.strict = true`, unit tests (layer `test`) may
not import concrete adapter modules; integration, contract, e2e, and
adapter tests belong in the `integration_test` layer (configurable via
`[layouts.<name>]`).

## Conventions

Naming that keeps decisions explicit. Configurable.

### LIT401

`boolean-policy`: A public core function takes a boolean, or returns one without a predicate name.

A `bool` parameter is a hidden mode switch; replace it with an enum or a
named value type. A function returning `bool` must be named as a question,
with one of the prefixes in `conventions.predicate_prefixes` (default `is_`,
`has_`, `can_`, `should_`, `allows_`, `contains_`, `matches_`). String
annotations, `Annotated`, unions, and local aliases are resolved. Private
functions are exempt.

### LIT402

`expected-outcome`: Core code raises or catches an expected outcome.

"Not found", "denied" or "expired" are ordinary results of a decision, not
failures. Exceptions whose names end with a suffix from
`conventions.outcome_suffixes` (default `NotFound`, `AlreadyExists`,
`Conflict`, `Denied`, `Expired`, `Forbidden`, `Rejected`, `Unauthorized`,
`Unavailable`) may not be raised or caught in core modules; return a named
result type instead.

### LIT403

`restricted-subclassing`: A class extends a base that is not on the allowlist.

Inheritance couples a class to its parent's internals; prefer composition,
functions over values, and `Protocol`s for shared interfaces. A class may
extend a name in `conventions.allowed_bases` (default: every builtin, such
as `Exception`, plus `typing.Protocol`/`NamedTuple`/`TypedDict`/`Generic`,
`enum` bases, Pydantic `BaseModel`/`RootModel`/`BaseSettings`, and
SQLAlchemy declarative bases and `TypeDecorator`), or a workspace class that
directly extends one: a shared `Base(DeclarativeBase)` for tables, a common
`Model(BaseModel)`, a `DomainError(Exception)`, or a `Protocol` a fake
implements. Deeper hierarchies are reported, except for exceptions, which
may nest to any depth. A table that extends a declarative base may also mix
in plain workspace classes, such as a `ProjectOwned` holding shared columns.
Entries ending in `.*` allow a whole module. Set `conventions.allowed_bases`
to replace the list, or `conventions.extend_allowed_bases` to add to it.

### LIT404

`core-classes`: Core code defines plain behavior classes, or (in strict mode) methods on records.

Core modules should model data as frozen dataclasses, `NamedTuple`s, or
enums and express behavior as pure module-level functions. Plain classes
without a data/protocol/exception role are always reported. With
`workspace.strict = true`, public instance methods on core records
(outside `@property`, `@cached_property`, `@classmethod`, and
`@staticmethod`) are also reported.

### LIT405

`core-exceptions`: Core code raises exceptions outside `__post_init__` (opt-in via `workspace.strict`).

Enabled with `workspace.strict = true`. Core functions compute total
decisions over typed values and return named results. Raise exceptions only
for construction invariants inside `__post_init__` (or `AssertionError` /
`NotImplementedError` guards); handle operational failures at edges.
Expected-outcome exceptions remain reported under LIT402.

### LIT406

`explicit-arguments`: Public core/port signatures or records define defaults (opt-in via `workspace.strict`).

Enabled with `workspace.strict = true`. Default values hide caller
obligations and let refactors silently drop arguments. Make callers pass
every argument on public core and port functions and every core/port record
field explicitly. Private helpers, lambdas, Protocol methods, exception
`__init__` methods, `ClassVar` attributes, and `field(init=False)` fields
are exempt.
